title: Track Selection — Binding Rationale
description:
This is the last thing you write as a foundation intern.

Choose one track — **SOC Analysis**, **Ethical Hacking**, or **GRC** — and write a rationale for your selection that would convince a sceptical senior. You may only pick one, and once graded the selection is final.

**Submission: in-platform** (this is narrative, no tables — the writeup pad handles this well, and we want the decision rationale visible inside the platform for downstream pairing with mentors).

**Your rationale must address, in order:**

  1. **The specific work from Stages 0–3 where you felt most alive.** Name the task by stage and number, name what clicked. Generic 'I enjoyed the technical tasks' answers lose 10 pts.
  2. **The specific work you found tedious.** Be honest about it; evaluators distrust candidates who claim to have loved everything equally. Name a stage and a task.
  3. **A one-year professional goal inside your chosen track** — concrete enough that failure would be visible. (Bad: 'become a strong SOC analyst'. Better: 'in 12 months, take primary on-call rotation for at least one SOC tier-2 shift per week, with mean-time-to-triage under 20 minutes on benign-vs-malicious classification'.)
  4. **One skill gap you will close in the first 90 days of track specialisation, and how.** Name the resource — course, lab, book, mentor, professional community. Vague answers lose 5 pts.
  5. **A sentence naming the other two tracks and why they are not your fit** — written without dismissal. 'GRC is boring' loses 10 pts. 'GRC requires patience for stakeholder management I do not yet have' is honest.

**Citation bar (lighter than other Stage 4 tasks — this is reflection, not external research):**
- Cite at least one task by Stage/task number where you formed the opinion in §1.
- Cite at least one external resource you've already started using (book, course, mentor, professional community) — be specific.
- One mention of the TRAN track curriculum if relevant.

**Scoring:** self-awareness is rewarded more than polish. Generic rationales that would apply to any candidate earn partial credit only. Evaluators look for evidence you have read your own work from Stages 1–3 and drawn a conclusion from it — not evidence you read a careers blog.

Keep the whole piece **under 500 words**. The chair reads the last paragraph first.

**One mistake I almost made:** 50+ word section. The seductive wrong answer is picking the track that scored best in your most recent stage instead of the track that fits your durable interest. Name the specific moment you nearly mis-picked and how you corrected it.

---

**Universal grading rule.** Generic answers fail. Every claim in your submission must be tied to specific evidence — an artefact from the lab (file path, log line, command output, payload, screenshot) **and** at least one external citation where research is relevant (NIST section number, MITRE technique ID, CVE, vendor advisory, ISO control ID, NDPA section). Claims without an attached artefact, timestamp, payload, standard section, or business constraint earn zero for that claim. Lab-only answers earn partial credit. External-only answers earn partial credit. Full credit requires both.
